lotl.label: What's Going On With the Leafs
lotl.body: The season didn't just end - it unraveled, and the numbers say it plainly: 32-36-14, 8th in the Atlantic Division, a bleak 78 points and a final seven-game skid that left the Maple Leafs 31 games adrift. Yet the real story now is the reset, not the wreckage. Toronto hired Jim Hiller as head coach, a move that feels less like a clean break than a fresh coat of paint on a house the club still insists it can sell as a contender. Hiller arrives with the reputation of a teacher who wants the game played with more bite and more joy - a useful trait in a room that has looked tight and joyless when the pressure spikes. The Leafs also remain tied to the Bruce Cassidy chatter, and that alone tells you this front office is still hunting for a sharper edge. What matters next is whether this becomes a true reckoning - coaching staff, free agency, and the roster's old vanity - or just another summer of rearranging the deck chairs.

lotl.label: What's Going On With the Jays
lotl.body: The Jays have spent the last two nights trading punches with Boston and, for once, landing the cleaner ones - the 3-0 blanking at Fenway on Wednesday gave them a second straight win and a little breathing room after a bruising pair of losses to the Yankees. At 36-38, they sit third in the AL East, 10 games back, a record that says contender on paper and chaser in practice. Still, there was edge in the way they handled the Red Sox: the bullpen day worked, the shutout held, and the club looked sharper than it did during the 8-3 loss on Sunday. That matters for a team trying to climb out of the division mud. Vladimir Guerrero Jr. remains the engine, and the lineup is finally giving him some help instead of asking him to drag the whole club by himself. The trick now is persistence, not flashes. They'll try to make it three straight this afternoon at 12:35 against Boston, and the Jays need the same disciplined pitching to prove this burst is a turn, not a tease.

lotl.label: What's Going On With the Raptors
lotl.body: The spring ended with a decent record and an unfinished feel - the kind of season that earns applause in April and hard questions in June. Toronto closed at 46-36, good for third in the Atlantic Division, but the ledger also says what everyone can see: this was a club good enough to matter, not yet sharp enough to threaten. The real story now is the draft board, where Toronto sits at No. 19 and No. 50 and is openly eyeing Labaron Philon. That tracks with the larger theme around the Raptors: they can afford to play the long game with RJ Barrett, keep building around younger talent, and resist the temptation to patch every hole at once. The postseason glow is gone, and so is any illusion that one tidy move fixes the whole job. The front office has to get the next swing right - especially in a draft shaped by NIL realities and a talent pool that may force patience. What matters next is whether Toronto turns those two picks into a guard who changes the room.

lotl.label: What's Going On With the Commanders
lotl.body: Something is already taking shape in Ashburn, and it starts with the young quarterback acting like a grown-up and the rookie back refusing to be just another name on the depth chart. Jayden Daniels has ramped up his leadership entering 2026, while Bill Croskey-Merritt is pushing to level up in minicamp - exactly the kind of early-summer heat this team needs. Washington finished last season 3rd in the NFC East, 6 games behind, and the record tells you there is still ground to cover even if the building feels brighter than it did a year ago. The more interesting story, though, is how this roster is being remade around Daniels' voice and the new pieces around him. Croskey-Merritt's urgency matters because backfields are won in June before they are won in September. So does the quiet work of integrating the receiver room and sorting out who belongs in the passing game now that the staff is testing roles instead of merely handing them out. What to watch next: whether Daniels' command keeps spreading and Croskey-Merritt turns minicamp buzz into a real grip on the offense.
